title: What the Transfer Portal Can Teach CEOs
author: Managing the Future
summary: Managing the Future draws a direct analogy between college football's transfer portal, where programs now onboard dozens of new players in months rather than developing them over years, and the challenge CEOs face onboarding AI agents that arrive with enormous raw capability but zero knowledge of how a specific organization actually operates. The piece argues that just as a coach must make strategy, language, standards, and responsibilities explicit for incoming transfer players, a company must document its own operating system before AI can be genuinely useful rather than merely polished and wrong. Its sharpest point reframes AI's much-discussed alignment problem as something every CEO now faces in miniature: powerful agents will execute confidently in the wrong direction unless the company's value-creation model, priorities, and decision rights have been written down. The author's closing test - how quickly could you get a brilliant stranger productive on Monday morning - is offered as a direct proxy for how AI-ready a company actually is, since a documented operating system, not access to AI tools themselves, is what competitors cannot copy.
points: Uses the specific scale of college football's transfer portal (10,500+ players moved in a 15-day window, Oklahoma State losing 64 and gaining 54) to make concrete just how compressed onboarding timelines have become, then maps that compression directly onto AI agent deployment.

Names the four things a coach must make explicit for a transfer player - strategy, language, standards, responsibilities - as a direct, reusable checklist for what a company must document before AI can operate inside it usefully.

Reframes AI's abstract 'alignment problem' (ensuring a powerful system pursues intended goals) as a concrete, practical problem every CEO already faces at the organizational level, not just a frontier AI-safety concern.

Identifies the real competitive moat in the AI era as the documented, distinctive operating system itself, not the AI tools, since competitors can buy the same AI but cannot copy a company's specific strategy, values, and decision rights.

Converts the entire argument into a single practical diagnostic question - how fast could a brilliant stranger become useful at your company - that a leader can apply immediately without needing to understand AI technically.
quotes: More than 10,500 players across NCAA divisions entered the transfer portal during the 15-day window in January. Oklahoma State lost 64 players and brought in 54.

CEOs face a similar challenge, not with free agents but with AI agents. Business leaders have suddenly gained access to an enormous amount of intelligence and capability. But like a transfer player, AI arrives knowing nothing about how your particular organization operates.

A coach cannot assume that new players understand how his program works. He has to make the important things explicit: Strategy, what are we trying to do, and how do we expect to win? Language, what do our terms and signals mean? Standards, what does good performance look like here? Responsibilities, who owns what, and how do we work together?

the AI does not automatically understand how your company creates value, which customers matter most, what tradeoffs you are willing to make, how your executives divide responsibility, or why a decision that looks sensible on paper will never work inside your organization
Unless that knowledge has been clearly articulated and recorded, AI goes to work without it. The result may be polished, impressive, and totally useless.
Your competitors can buy the same AI tools. They cannot copy the operating system you have built around your particular strategy, people, customers, and way of working.

Imagine that a brilliant stranger joins your company Monday morning. How quickly could you teach that person enough about the business to produce useful work? Your answer is a good indication of how ready your company is for AI.
